text: More than 400 years ago, the Lakota, whose name means “allies”, lived near the upper Mississippi River.
Then Cree fighters with iron weapons pushed them west onto the Great Plains.
src: In the late 16th and early 17th centuries Dakota and Lakota speakers lived in the upper Mississippi region / Their name means “allies”
until Cree war parties armed with iron weapons pushed them west onto the Great Plains

text: The Lakota got horses from the Cheyenne and became riders who hunted bison on the Plains.
In summer their tipis stood in great circles, which they called the sacred hoop of the nation.
src: In the early 18th century the Lakota obtained horses from the Cheyenne along the Missouri River / On the Plains the Lakota became a horse-mounted, bison-hunting people
a great summer gathering for ceremony and the communal hunt, when the tipi circles formed what the Lakota called the sacred hoop of the nation

text: About 250 years ago they made the Black Hills their home, and these hills are sacred to them.
Their stories tell of White Buffalo Calf Woman, who gave the people a sacred pipe.
src: made the Black Hills their home by the 1770s / The Black Hills are sacred to the Lakota
White Buffalo Calf Woman, Ptesáŋwiŋ, gave the people the sacred buffalo calf pipe

text: A treaty kept settlers out of the Black Hills, but then gold was found there and miners poured in.
War followed, and the Lakota and Cheyenne won the Battle of the Little Bighorn.
src: The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty closed the Black Hills to white settlement, but after gold was found there in 1874 / prospectors poured in
war followed / Lakota and Cheyenne forces under Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull defeat Custer at the Battle of the Little Bighorn

text: But the army broke their resistance, and later the Lakota leader Sitting Bull was killed.
Soon after, soldiers killed at least 270 Lakota at Wounded Knee, many of them women and children.
src: A winter campaign broke the remaining resistance / In December 1890 Sitting Bull was killed at Standing Rock
two weeks later the 7th Cavalry, with Hotchkiss guns, killed at least 270 Lakota of Spotted Elk’s band at Wounded Knee Creek, about 170 of them women and children

text: Today most Lakota live on five reservations, lands set aside for them, in South Dakota, and some speak their language, Lakȟótiyapi.
They still refuse money for the Black Hills, because taking it would end their claim to the land.
src: Today the Lakota live mainly on five reservations in South Dakota / about 2,000 of whom spoke Lakȟótiyapi
The tribes refused the $122 million that the Supreme Court awarded for the Black Hills in 1980, as accepting it would end their claim
